title: À la recherche de Mr. Dinosaure - one-minute example

links.note: `Qu'est-ce qu'il y a` = what's wrong / what's the matter, literally “what is it that there is?”: `est → être`, third-person singular present indicative; `il y a` = there is, with `a → avoir`, third-person singular present indicative and the dummy subject `il`. With a person named after it, it asks what is wrong with them.
`Georges` = George, the person asked.

line.source: Eh bien, Georges, qu'est-ce qu'il t'arrive ?
line.translation: Well, George, what's wrong with you?
notes: This line and the previous `Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ?` both ask what is wrong. This version builds on `arriver à`: literally “what is it that is happening to you?”, with `t'` (to you) receiving the happening.

links.note: `Eh bien` = well, a discourse marker opening the reply.
`Georges` = George, the person addressed.

`qu'est-ce qu'il t'arrive` = what's happening to you / what's wrong with you, literally “what is it that arrives to you?”: `arrive → arriver`, third-person singular present indicative with the dummy subject `il`. `T'` = `te` (to you) elided before a vowel, the indirect object — the person the thing happens to. `Arriver à quelqu'un` = to happen to someone.
`Dinosaur !` = “Dinosaur!” — George's tearful cry: the lost toy is all he can say.

line.source: Oh non, ne me dis pas que tu as perdu Monsieur Dinosaur.
line.translation: Oh no, don't tell me you've lost Mister Dinosaur.
notes: In the negative imperative the pronoun stays before the verb — `ne me dis pas` — while the affirmative form attaches it after with a hyphen: `dis-moi`, heard later in this episode.

source: que tu as perdu Monsieur Dinosaur.

links.note: `Oh non` = oh no; `non` = no.

`ne me dis pas` = don't tell me. `Dis → dire`, second-person singular imperative used negatively: `ne ... pas` wraps the verb, and the indirect object `me` (to me) stays in front of it. `Ne me dis pas que...` is a set frame for dismay about the news in the `que`-clause.

`que tu as perdu Monsieur Dinosaur` = (that) you've lost Mister Dinosaur. `Que` = that, introducing what must not be said; `as perdu → perdre`, passé composé with `as → avoir` (second-person singular present) + `perdu` (past participle) = have lost; `tu` = you, the subject.
`Georges` = George, the subject.

`a perdu → perdre`, passé composé, third-person singular: `a` = the auxiliary `avoir` in the present + `perdu`, the past participle = has lost. The loss is complete and its result stands now: the toy is missing.
`Monsieur Dinosaur` = Mister Dinosaur, the direct object — the thing lost.

line.source: Ne t'inquiète pas, on va t'aider à le retrouver.
line.translation: Don't worry, we'll help you find him.
notes: `On` does the job of `nous` for “we” in everyday French and takes a singular verb: `on va` = we're going to.
Three verb levels stack: `va` (going to) + `t'aider` (help you) + `à le retrouver` (to find him). Each governing verb keeps the next one in the infinitive.

links.note: `Ne t'inquiète pas` = don't worry. `T'inquiète → s'inquiéter`, second-person singular imperative, negative: the verb is pronominal, so the reflexive `te` (yourself, elided to `t'`) stays before the verb, with `ne ... pas` around it — literally “don't worry yourself”.

`on va t'aider` = we'll help you. `On` = we in everyday speech; `va → aller`, third-person singular present indicative agreeing with `on`; `aller + infinitive` = going to / will; `t'aider → aider` (to help) stays an infinitive, with `te` (you) as its object placed before it.

`à le retrouver` = to find him. `Aider à + infinitive` = to help do something; `retrouver` = to find again, get back (`re-` = again + `trouver`, to find); `le` = him, standing for Monsieur Dinosaur, before the infinitive.

line.source: Ça, c'est le travail d'un bon détective.
line.translation: That's the job of a good detective.
notes: The fronted `ça` is picked up by `c'est`: literally “that, it is the job of a good detective”. Dropping the announcement gives the ordinary order `c'est le travail d'un bon détective`.

links.note: `Ça, c'est` = that's / that is. `Ça` = that, an informal demonstrative, fronted and then picked up by `c'` in `c'est` — `est → être`, third-person singular present indicative with subject `ce`.
`le travail` = the job / the work; `travail` = work.
`d'un bon détective` = of a good detective: `d'un` = `de + un` (of a); `bon` = good; `détective` = detective.

notes: `C'est quoi` puts the question word after the statement frame `c'est`: informal but the usual spoken pattern. A neutral written version is `Qu'est-ce qu'un détective ?`.

links.note: `Papa` = Daddy, the person asked.
`c'est quoi` = what is: an informal spoken question that keeps the statement frame `c'est` (`est → être`, third-person singular present indicative) and adds `quoi` (what) after it.
`un détective` = a detective: `un` = a, the masculine article.

line.source: Un détective, c'est une personne très importante parce qu'il peut retrouver n'importe quoi.
line.translation: A detective is a very important person because he can find anything.
notes: The definition pattern `un détective, c'est...` announces the word first and then defines it with `c'est` plus a description — the everyday way to define something, instead of the flatter `un détective est une personne...`.

links.note: `Un détective` = a detective — the word being defined, announced first.
`c'est` = is: `est → être`, third-person singular present indicative with subject `ce`; its real subject here is the fronted `un détective`.
`une personne très importante` = a very important person. `Personne` = person, a feminine noun; `très` = very; `importante` = important, feminine singular agreeing with `personne`.

`parce qu'il peut retrouver` = because he can find. `Parce que` = because (`parce qu'` before a vowel); `peut → pouvoir`, third-person singular present indicative = can, is able to; `retrouver` = to find, an infinitive after the modal `peut`; `il` = he, referring to the detective.
`n'importe quoi` = anything, literally “no matter what”: a fixed expression from `n'importe` (no matter) + `quoi` (what).

line.source: Moi, moi, moi, moi aussi je peux trouver n'importe quoi.
line.translation: Me, me, me! I can find anything too!
notes: `Moi aussi` doubles the subject: the stressed `moi` emphasizes who is included, and `je` just after resumes that person as the grammatical subject. Ordinary order: `je peux aussi trouver...`.

links.note: `Moi, moi, moi` = me, me, me: `moi` is the stressed pronoun for me, used on its own when shouting to be picked.
`moi aussi` = me too: `aussi` = too, as well. The stressed `moi` emphasizes who is included, and the subject `je` just after resumes the same person.

`je peux trouver n'importe quoi` = I can find anything. `Peux → pouvoir`, first-person singular present indicative = can; `trouver` = to find, an infinitive after the modal; `n'importe quoi` = anything, literally “no matter what”.

line.source: C'est entendu, ce sera Peppa notre détective.
line.translation: All right then, Peppa will be our detective.
notes: `Ce sera Peppa notre détective` states the choice and then appends her role with no connecting verb: literally “it will be Peppa, our detective”. English needs “Peppa will be our detective”.

links.note: `C'est entendu` = agreed / all right then / it's settled. `Est → être`, third-person singular present indicative with subject `ce`; `entendu` = the past participle of `entendre` (to hear) inside this fixed phrase — “heard and accepted”.
`ce sera Peppa` = Peppa will be, literally “it will be Peppa”. `Sera → être`, third-person singular future, with subject `ce`; the person chosen follows the verb.
`notre détective` = our detective: `notre` = our; `détective` = detective.

line.source: Georges, c'est moi la détective. Je vais t'aider à retrouver Monsieur Dinosaur.
line.translation: George, I'm the detective. I'll help you find Mister Dinosaur.
notes: `C'est moi la détective` insists on who: the ordinary order is `je suis la détective`. The `c'est moi` pattern puts the stress on the person.

links.note: `Georges` = George, the person addressed.
`c'est moi` = I'm / it's me: `est → être`, third-person singular present indicative with subject `ce`; `moi` = me, the stressed pronoun naming who is meant.

`la détective` = the detective. The feminine article `la` marks that the detective is a girl (Peppa); both `le détective` and `la détective` occur for a woman, and the noun's spelling does not change.

`Je vais t'aider` = I'll help you / I'm going to help you. `Vais → aller`, first-person singular present indicative; `aller + infinitive` expresses what is about to happen; `t'aider → aider` (to help) stays an infinitive, with `te` (you) placed before it.
`à retrouver Monsieur Dinosaur` = to find Mister Dinosaur: `aider à + infinitive` again; `retrouver` = to find again, get back.

line.source: La détective devrait peut-être commencer par poser à Georges des questions simples.
line.translation: The detective should perhaps start by asking George some simple questions.
notes: Three verbs stack: `devrait` (should) is conjugated, `commencer` (to start) is its infinitive, and `poser` (to ask) is in turn governed by `commencer par` — start by asking.

links.note: `La détective` = the detective — Peppa, the subject.
`devrait peut-être` = should perhaps. `Devrait → devoir`, third-person singular conditional = should, ought to; `peut-être` = maybe, a fixed adverb placed inside the verb group here.
`commencer par` = start by: `commencer` = to start, an infinitive after `devrait`; `commencer par + infinitive` = to begin by doing something.

`poser à Georges` = asking George: `poser` = to put, to pose, an infinitive after `par`; `poser une question à quelqu'un` = to ask someone a question, with the person marked by `à` — `à Georges` = to George.
`des questions simples` = some simple questions: `des` = some; `questions` = questions; `simples` = simple, placed after the noun it describes.

line.source: Georges, il est où Monsieur Dinosaur ?
notes: The pronoun `il` comes before the name it stands for: literally “he is where, Mister Dinosaur?”. Spoken French often announces the pronoun first and names the person after; English must wait for the name.
`Il est où` keeps statement order, with `où` left after the verb — the informal spoken way to ask. Formal French fronts it: `où est Monsieur Dinosaur ?`.

links.note: `Georges` = George, the person addressed.
`il est où` = where is (he/it): `est → être`, third-person singular present indicative; `où` = where, left after the verb. `Il` = he/it, standing for the toy.
`Monsieur Dinosaur ?` = Mister Dinosaur, named after the pronoun that stands for him.

line.source: Georges ne sait pas où se trouve Monsieur Dinosaur.
line.translation: George doesn't know where Mister Dinosaur is.
notes: Inside the `où`-clause the subject follows the verb: `où se trouve Monsieur Dinosaur` = where Mister Dinosaur is located. That inversion is normal in indirect questions; English keeps the subject before “is”.

links.note: `Georges` = George, the subject.
`ne sait pas` = doesn't know. `Sait → savoir`, third-person singular present indicative, negated with `ne ... pas`; `savoir` = to know a fact.

`où se trouve Monsieur Dinosaur` = where Mister Dinosaur is. `Où` = where, introducing the indirect question; `se trouve → se trouver`, third-person singular present indicative, literally “finds itself” = is located; its subject, `Monsieur Dinosaur`, comes after the verb.
